who: A very old woman, stooped and slow, who has lived in the same house longer than anyone else in the village.
place: Her own kitchen, at dusk, the fire burned low and no one else in the house.
present: a pot left boiling on the fire
a walking stick propped by the door
a neighbor's dog scratching at the yard gate

factors.fact: She has stirred that pot at this hour every day for sixty years, long after the need for it passed.
Her knees no longer bend without pain, and the stairs to the loft are hard to climb.
She is afraid of admitting she has forgotten the name of the neighbor whose dog is barking.
The dog's bark is the same pitch as one she raised as a girl, and for a moment she is certain it is that dog.
She promised her daughter she would eat supper before dark, and it is nearly dark now.
Her hands still know the motions of cooking even when her mind wanders.

does.verb: stirs the pot and talks to the dog as if it were the one she raised as a girl

could_also.verb: calls out for her daughter
sits down by the fire and forgets the pot
goes to let the dog in

would_not.verb: climbs to the loft
would_not.why: her knees would not carry her and she knows it even when her mind wanders

would_not.verb: leaves the pot to go outside in the cold
would_not.why: the promise to her daughter about supper holds even when the memory of the dog does not

then: She keeps stirring until the pot boils dry, then startles at the smell and only then remembers where she is.
why: The old habit of the pot and the promise to her daughter pull her to stay at the fire, while the sound of the dog pulls her thirty years into a memory; her body settles it, since standing to go outside costs more than staying does.
turns_on: whether the dog stays quiet or barks again

who: A small child, barely past toddling, left to play while the adults work nearby.
place: The riverbank below the washing stones, midmorning, the water low and slow after a dry spell.
present: two women washing clothes upstream
a smooth flat stone at the water's edge
a duckling paddling alone near the reeds

factors.fact: The duckling's movement is the brightest, closest thing to watch.
The child has never been told the river drops away past the flat stone, and would not understand the words yet if told.
The child is hungry and has been fussy since before noon.
The women's voices are close enough to hear but not close enough to reach quickly.
The child only learned to stand without holding on to something two weeks ago.

does.verb: totters toward the duckling at the water's edge

could_also.verb: sits down and cries for food
picks up the flat stone to look at it
wanders toward the women's voices instead

would_not.verb: stops at the water's edge on purpose
would_not.why: it has no sense yet of where the safe ground ends

would_not.verb: calls out a warning to itself
would_not.why: it does not yet have words for danger, only for wanting

then: It reaches the edge of the flat stone and leans after the duckling; one of the women looks up in time to shout and run.
why: The bright moving duckling pulls harder on a child this young than hunger does, and the new balance to walk gives it just enough reach to follow that pull past the point an adult would call safe.
turns_on: how far the duckling drifts from the bank

who: A grown man laid up with a fever that has not broken in three days.
place: A small bedroom at midday, shutters closed against the light, the household going about its work outside the door.
present: a bowl of water and a cloth by the bed
his wife's voice through the wall
a jug of the strong drink he keeps for pain

factors.fact: The fever makes him thirsty in a way that plain water does not satisfy.
He has started mistaking his wife's voice through the wall for his dead brother's.
He does not want anyone to see him confused, and would rather they think he is only resting.
The healer told him plainly that the strong drink would make the fever worse, not better.
He can sit up but standing makes the room tilt.

does.verb: lies still and answers the wall as if it were his brother
does.toward: his wife's voice through the wall

could_also.verb: calls out for water
could_also.toward: his wife's voice through the wall

could_also.verb: reaches for the jug despite the warning
tries to sit up and go to the door

would_not.verb: gets up and walks outside
would_not.why: the tilt in the room when he stands is worse than the confusion he can hide lying down

would_not.verb: tells his wife what he is hearing
would_not.why: the wish not to be seen confused outweighs the comfort of saying it aloud

then: He drifts between answering the wall and dozing until his wife comes in with water and he goes quiet, unsure afterward what he said.
why: The fever's thirst pushes him toward the jug, but the healer's warning and the last of his sense hold him to plain water; the confusion about the voice wins out over both because it comes from inside, where warnings do not reach.
turns_on: whether the fever breaks before the jug is reached

who: A man who has had far more of the strong drink than he is used to, well after dark.
place: The lane outside the tavern, late at night, most windows dark, a low wall running along one side.
present: a low wall along the lane
a stray cat sitting on the wall
his own house, three doors further on, dark

factors.fact: His balance is gone enough that the ground feels like it tilts.
The cat sitting still and looking at him feels, in the moment, like good company.
He knows his own door by shape more than by thought, three doors down.
His wife told him plainly not to be late again.
The drink has made small things, like the cat, feel far more important than they are.

does.verb: stops to talk to the cat on the wall

could_also.verb: leans on the wall to steady himself
tries to pick up the cat
gives up and sits down in the lane

would_not.verb: walks straight home without stopping
would_not.why: the drink has drowned out the sense that would make him hurry

would_not.verb: argues loudly for a long time
would_not.why: even drunk, a stray cat holds his attention only a little while before he loses the thread

then: The cat slips away when he reaches for it, and he stands blinking before remembering, slowly, that he was going somewhere.
why: The wife's warning is the stronger claim by daylight, but the drink has weakened everything except what is right in front of him, so the cat wins his attention until it leaves and there is nothing left to hold it.
turns_on: whether the cat stays on the wall or slips away

who: A workhorse that has pulled a loaded cart uphill since before dawn without rest.
place: The top of a long hill road, midafternoon, the cart still half full, the stable still an hour's walk off.
present: the driver holding the reins
the loaded cart behind it
a patch of shade under a lone tree at the roadside

factors.fact: Its legs are trembling in a way they were not an hour ago.
It has pulled this same road for years and knows the stable is close once the hill ends.
It has not had water since the morning and the day is hot.
The driver is tapping the reins for it to keep moving.
The shade under the tree is a few steps off the road.

does.verb: stops walking and will not go further

could_also.verb: veers toward the shade under the tree
keeps pulling at a slower pace
tosses its head against the reins

would_not.verb: bolts forward suddenly
would_not.why: it has no strength left in its legs to spend on a sudden run

would_not.verb: lies down in the road
would_not.why: even this tired, standing feels safer to it than being down where the cart could roll onto it

then: The driver eventually leads it to the shade and loosens the harness before it will move again, losing the better part of an hour.
why: Years of the same road tell it the stable is close, which would normally be enough to finish the pull, but the trembling in its legs and the thirst outweigh that habit today; the driver's tapping cannot substitute for water or rest.
turns_on: whether the driver lets it rest at the shade

who: A hunter who lost his sight to an illness two months ago and has not yet relearned his own house.
place: His own cottage, midmorning, the furniture recently moved by a well-meaning relative.
present: a low table moved from its old place
his hunting dog lying by the door
his sister's voice from the next room

factors.fact: He still walks the room by the map of where things used to stand.
He has started, without much success yet, to listen for the dog's breathing to find the door.
He does not want his sister to see him walk into the moved table again.
The table was moved yesterday and no one told him.
The dog has taken to standing between him and anything newly in his path.

does.verb: walks forward from memory and strikes his shin on the moved table

could_also.verb: stops and calls to his sister to ask what moved
reaches down to follow the dog's lead
stands still until someone notices

would_not.verb: admits out loud that he is disoriented
would_not.why: the hurt to his pride is fresher than the pain in his shin

would_not.verb: kicks the table over in anger
would_not.why: anger at the table would only confirm to his sister how much he has struggled, which he is trying to hide

then: He rubs his shin and mutters that he should be more careful, then works the new shape of the room into his memory before trying the walk again.
why: The old map of the room is stronger in his mind than any new habit of listening for the dog, so he trusts it until it fails him outright; pride keeps him from simply asking, even though asking would have cost him nothing.
turns_on: whether anyone warns him the table moved before he reaches it

who: A wolf raised from a cub by a shepherd family, grown now to full size and kept mostly as a working dog.
place: The sheep pen at dusk, the flock restless, a real wild wolf's howl carrying from the ridge above.
present: the flock of sheep in the pen
the shepherd calling from the house
the howl of a wild wolf on the ridge

factors.fact: It has slept by the shepherd's fire every night of its life and has never hunted for itself.
The howl on the ridge is answered, low in its chest, before it can stop itself.
It has guarded this flock since it was half-grown and does not think of the sheep as prey.
Something in the howl pulls at muscles it has never used on purpose.
The shepherd's voice is calling its name, the only word it has ever answered to.

does.verb: answers the shepherd's call and stays at the pen
does.toward: the shepherd calling from the house

could_also.verb: paces the fence line growling toward the ridge
howls back once before falling silent
herds the sheep tighter together

would_not.verb: leaves the pen to find the wild wolf
would_not.why: it has never once left the flock unwatched and the pull of the howl is not stronger than that habit yet

would_not.verb: attacks the sheep
would_not.why: it does not see them as prey, whatever its blood might want elsewhere

then: It stays at the fence through the night, restless and pacing, and answers the shepherd's call each time it is given, but sleeps badly.
why: The howl reaches something bred into it that a life by the fire never removed, but the years of guarding the flock and answering to the shepherd's voice are the stronger claim tonight; the pull is real without yet being enough.
turns_on: how many nights in a row the wild wolf howls

who: A dog that ran off from a farm a year ago and has lived wild in the woods since.
place: The edge of the woods near the farm at dusk, the farm gate visible, its old owner outside calling a name it once answered to.
present: the farm gate and yard, visible through the trees
its old owner calling from the yard
a rabbit's fresh trail crossing nearby

factors.kind: what it has learned to fear
factors.fact: A year of finding its own food and shelter has made it wary of anything that once meant a chain or a shed.
The sound of that particular voice still loosens something in it that no other voice does.
It is thinner than it was on the farm and the winter ahead will be harder than the last.

factors.kind: what its body is trained for now
factors.fact: It has learned to read a fresh trail like the rabbit's without thinking about it.

factors.kind: what people mean to it now
factors.fact: The last two people it came near threw stones at it.

does.verb: stays at the tree line, watching, and does not come closer

could_also.verb: follows the rabbit's trail instead
circles closer under cover before losing its nerve
slinks away deeper into the woods

would_not.verb: runs straight to the owner as it once did
would_not.why: a year of thrown stones from other people has worn down the trust that used to be automatic

would_not.verb: barks to announce itself
would_not.why: barking would give away a position it has learned, hard, not to give away

then: It watches until the owner gives up calling and goes back inside, then noses along the rabbit's trail once the yard is quiet again.
why: The old voice still pulls, more than any other sound would, but a year of learning that people mean danger now outweighs it; the trail offers something certain where the yard only offers a memory.
turns_on: whether the old owner comes out into the open unarmed and alone

who: A young deer that has never come across a person before, born and raised in a stretch of forest people rarely enter.
place: A clearing at the forest's edge, late afternoon, where a stranger has been standing motionless for hours.
present: the stranger standing still at the clearing's edge
the deer's mother grazing nearby
a stream running along the clearing

factors.fact: Nothing in its life has taught it that an upright, still shape means danger.
The shape has not moved, made a sound, or given off a smell it recognizes as predator in all the time it has watched.
It is thirsty and the stream runs closer to the stranger than it would like.
Its mother has gone on grazing without alarm, which it takes as a sign.
Nothing has ever taught it to be curious about something so still, only that stillness is not moving.

does.verb: edges closer to drink at the stream, watching the stranger the whole time

could_also.verb: stays beside its mother and does not approach
circles wide around the stranger to reach the stream
freezes and watches without drinking

would_not.verb: bolts away at first sight of the stranger
would_not.why: nothing has taught it to associate a still, silent shape with danger, so there is no reason yet to run

would_not.verb: walks directly up to touch the stranger
would_not.why: even without learned fear, an untried shape this size is approached only as far as thirst requires

then: It drinks in short bursts, lifting its head to watch the stranger between swallows, and drifts off with its mother once its thirst is settled.
why: Thirst and its mother's calm both pull it toward the water, and nothing in its experience pulls the other way since the stranger has given off none of the signs it knows to fear; only the plain unfamiliarity of the shape keeps it cautious rather than careless.
turns_on: whether the stranger moves suddenly while it drinks

who: A householder returning home to find a stranger already inside, holding one of her own kitchen knives and turning it over in the light.
place: Her own kitchen, early evening, the door left unlatched while she fetched water.
present: the stranger holding her kitchen knife
the open door behind the stranger
her own walking stick by the door, within reach

factors.fact: The knife the stranger is holding is one she uses every day and knows the weight of.
She has never seen this person before and has no idea what they want.
Her walking stick is by the door, closer to her than to the stranger.
The stranger is turning the knife over slowly, looking at it with plain curiosity rather than menace, and has not moved toward her.
She is alone in the house and the nearest neighbor is a shout away, maybe more.

does.verb: stands in the doorway and demands to know what they are doing with her knife
does.toward: the stranger holding her kitchen knife

could_also.verb: backs out to call for the neighbor
reaches for the walking stick before speaking
orders them out of the house
could_also.toward: the stranger holding her kitchen knife

would_not.verb: attacks the stranger outright
would_not.toward: the stranger holding her kitchen knife
would_not.why: the stranger's calm, curious handling of the knife gives her no sign of a real attack coming, so going straight to force is more risk than the moment calls for

would_not.verb: ignores it and starts on supper
would_not.why: a stranger holding her knife in her own kitchen is not a thing she can simply work around

then: The stranger sets the knife down at her sharp word and stands there, unbothered, waiting to see what she does next, which unsettles her more than if they had run.
why: What is hers and what she does not know both push her to challenge the stranger at once, while the stranger's calm manner and her nearness to the stick both weigh against jumping straight to force; the challenge in the doorway does the most with the least risk.
turns_on: whether the stranger sets the knife down when challenged

who: A market trader whose regular customer notices a stranger standing far closer than anyone normally does, then following her stall to stall.
place: The market square at midday, crowded, the stranger a step behind her at every turn.
present: the crowd of the market
her own stall, unattended while she walks
another trader she knows two stalls down

factors.fact: No one she knows stands this close without a reason, and this person has given none.
The market is crowded enough that raising her voice would draw eyes fast.
Her own stall is sitting unwatched while she is followed away from it.
The stranger has said nothing and made no move to touch her or take anything, only kept the same short distance.
The trader two stalls down has known her for years and would come if called.

does.verb: moves toward the trader she knows and stays near him
does.toward: the trader she knows two stalls down

could_also.verb: turns and asks the stranger directly what they want
cuts back through the crowd to lose them
hurries back to her unattended stall

would_not.verb: ignores it and keeps wandering the market alone
would_not.why: the closeness feels wrong enough that being alone with it is not something she is willing to keep doing

would_not.verb: shouts for help without trying anything else first
would_not.why: the stranger has done nothing yet worth the scene that shouting would cause in a crowd this size

then: She reaches the trader and stands beside him, and the stranger stops a little further back, still watching, until she decides whether to go back for her stall.
why: The wrongness of the closeness and the risk to her unattended stall pull in opposite directions, but neither the stranger's silence nor the crowd gives her a clean way to confront it, so she moves to where she has help without yet making a scene.
turns_on: whether the stranger closes the distance again once she reaches the trader

who: A trader at his stall approached by a stranger offering a handful of ordinary river stones for a good working axe.
place: The trader's stall at the edge of the market, midafternoon, a small line of other customers waiting.
present: the axe on the stall
the handful of river stones the stranger is offering
a line of other customers waiting

factors.fact: The axe took him half a season's coin to have made, and the stones are worth nothing he can use.
Other customers are waiting and watching this go on.
The stranger holds the stones out plainly, as if certain they are a fair offer, with no sign of a joke.
He is known in this market for driving a hard but fair bargain, and other traders are watching.
He has no way to tell if the stranger is simple-minded, testing him, or means something by the stones he cannot see.

does.verb: refuses the trade and tells the stranger plainly what the axe is worth
does.toward: the stranger offering the river stones

could_also.verb: laughs it off and waves the next customer forward
asks the stranger where they got the idea the stones were worth anything
could_also.toward: the stranger offering the river stones

could_also.verb: offers a smaller, cheaper item for the stones instead
could_also.toward: the stranger offering the river stones

would_not.verb: accepts the trade as offered
would_not.toward: the stranger offering the river stones
would_not.why: half a season's coin is too much to give up on a trade this one-sided, whatever the stranger's reasons

would_not.verb: drives the stranger off with anger
would_not.toward: the stranger offering the river stones
would_not.why: the stranger has shown no malice, only a bad sense of value, which does not deserve anger in front of a line of watching customers

then: The stranger looks at the refused stones a moment, then puts them away and moves off without arguing, leaving him to wonder what that was about.
why: The axe's real worth and the watching line both push him to refuse plainly rather than humor the trade, while his uncertainty about the stranger's reasons and their evident lack of malice keep him from responding with more than a flat no.
turns_on: whether the stranger argues the value of the stones or simply moves on

who: A ferryman asked the same question about the river's depth by the same stranger for the fifth time in an hour.
place: The riverbank by the ferry landing, late morning, a small queue of other travelers waiting to cross.
present: the queue of travelers waiting to cross
the ferry tied at the landing
the river running past, its depth unchanged since the first time he answered

factors.fact: He has answered this exact question four times already, in the same words each time.
The queue behind the stranger is growing restless waiting to cross.
The stranger listens to each answer as though hearing it fresh, with no sign of mocking him or not understanding the words.
He is not a patient man on a good day, and this is not a good day.
He cannot tell whether the stranger is simple, deaf in a way that is not obvious, or testing him on purpose.

does.verb: answers a fifth time, more shortly than before
does.toward: the stranger asking about the river's depth

could_also.verb: waves the stranger onto the ferry without answering again
could_also.toward: the stranger asking about the river's depth

could_also.verb: turns to the next traveler in line instead
asks the stranger why they keep asking
could_also.toward: the stranger asking about the river's depth

would_not.verb: refuses to answer at all
would_not.toward: the stranger asking about the river's depth
would_not.why: the stranger has shown no sign of mockery, so refusing outright would be punishing something he cannot yet explain

would_not.verb: shouts at the stranger to make them stop
would_not.toward: the stranger asking about the river's depth
would_not.why: the queue watching would see more in that than the question deserves, and it would not make the next question less likely

then: He gives the fifth answer and turns straight to the queue, hoping the stranger boards without asking a sixth time; they do.
why: His own thinning patience and the growing queue both push him toward cutting the exchange short, but the stranger's genuine, unmocking manner keeps him from refusing outright; a short answer costs him less than either extreme.
turns_on: whether the stranger asks a sixth time

who: A farmer who spots a stranger crouched at the edge of his dry hay field, striking a small fire for no reason he can see.
place: The edge of his hay field at dusk, the hay cut and drying, dangerously close to catching.
present: the dry cut hay, close enough to catch
the small fire the stranger is building
his own well and bucket, some distance off

factors.fact: A season's cut hay is a few strides from that fire and dry enough to go up fast.
His well and bucket are a run away, not a step away.
The stranger is not hiding the fire or looking around as if to check for witnesses, only building it, plainly, as though it were an ordinary thing to do here.
There is no reason he can see for a fire in this spot at all, no food to cook, no cold to warm against in this weather.

factors.kind: what is owed to his family
factors.fact: His family's winter depends on that hay surviving to be gathered in.

does.verb: runs to stamp out the fire before it reaches the hay
does.toward: the small fire the stranger is building

could_also.verb: shouts at the stranger to stop while running
runs for the bucket and well first
grabs the stranger away from the fire bodily

would_not.verb: stops to ask the stranger's reasons first
would_not.why: the hay is too close and too dry to spend the time understanding a reason that plainly is not going to make sense

would_not.verb: walks over calmly assuming it will burn out on its own
would_not.why: dry hay this close to a fire is not a risk worth trusting to burn out by itself

then: He kicks the fire apart and stamps the last of it into the dirt, then rounds on the stranger, who watches him do it without protest or explanation.
why: The threat to his family's winter hay outweighs every question about why the stranger lit it at all, and the stranger's plain, unhidden manner rules out the slower approach of asking first; speed wins over understanding here.
turns_on: how close the fire has already gotten to the hay when he sees it

who: A traveler new to this village, still unsure of its customs, offered a good milking goat by a stranger for no price at all.
place: The village lane near the well, morning, several villagers nearby going about their errands.
present: the milking goat on its lead
several villagers going about their morning errands
the well at the center of the lane

factors.fact: She has been in this village only a week and does not yet know what a gift like this is supposed to mean here.
A milking goat is worth more than most people give away without expecting something back.
The stranger holds out the lead plainly, asking nothing in return and showing no sign of a trick.
She is afraid that accepting will put her in a debt she does not understand the shape of, by whatever custom governs it here.
The villagers nearby are watching the exchange without stepping in to explain either way.

does.verb: hesitates and asks the stranger what is expected in return before touching the lead

could_also.verb: refuses the goat outright
looks to the watching villagers for a sign of what to do
accepts the goat and thanks them plainly

would_not.verb: takes the goat without any question
would_not.why: not knowing the local custom around a gift this size, taking it without asking risks an obligation she cannot see the terms of

would_not.verb: assumes it must be some kind of trick and walks away at once
would_not.why: the stranger's plain, unpressuring manner gives her no real sign of a trick, only an unfamiliar generosity

then: The stranger says plainly that nothing is expected and sets the lead in her hand anyway, and she stands holding it, still unsure whether she has just accepted a kindness or a debt.
why: The goat's real worth pulls her to be cautious, since giving that much away for nothing runs against what she assumes any custom would ask, but the stranger's plain manner and the silence of the watching villagers give her no clear signal either way; she asks rather than guessing wrong in a place whose rules she does not know.
turns_on: whether any villager steps in to explain what such a gift means here
